lead.headline: A Titan Helicopter Practises on a Computer First
lead.deck: NASA's Dragonfly finished a pretend first flight. The real one is years away.
body: Pilots practise before a big flight. So do robots. NASA's Dragonfly is a rotorcraft, a flying machine with spinning blades. It will fly on Titan, a moon of Saturn. On 23 October NASA said it had finished its first flight, but only on a computer.
That pretend run is a simulation. In it, Dragonfly separated from its backshell. Then it flew over Titan's sand dunes. It scanned the terrain for a safe site. Then it circled back and landed.
Dragonfly will be on its own. Engineer Zach Putnam said, “Everything we do on Titan has to happen autonomously.” That means without a person steering.

science.headline: A Fast-Turning Space Telescope Says Goodbye
science.deck: NASA's Swift hunted giant explosions for 21 years. Its last observation was on 20 October.
body: Swift is a telescope that orbits Earth. It launched on 20 November 2004. NASA planned a two-year main mission, but Swift worked for more than 10 times that long.
Swift hunted gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the cosmos. It observed more than 2,000. It also studied more than 1,400 supernova explosions. A supernova is a star blowing up.
Speed was its skill. After it detected a burst, it could turn its telescopes to that spot in about a minute. In May 2005 it watched a short burst that lasted only 0.03 seconds.

Now Swift orbits below 275 kilometres. The air is thicker there, and stronger drag keeps its telescopes from holding steady. Drag is the slowing push of air. Its final observation was on 20 October 2026. NASA expects it to re-enter Earth's atmosphere within a few weeks.

world.headline: Early Warnings and School Shelters Help in Cyclone Arnab
world.deck: The storm crossed India's east coast on 28 October. Tens of thousands moved first.
body: A cyclone is a huge spinning storm with strong winds and heavy rain. Cyclone Arnab crossed the coast of Andhra Pradesh, in southeast India, on 28 October. India's weather office called it a very severe cyclonic storm. Gusts reached 150 kilometres an hour. A fast car on a highway goes about 100.

The storm's best defence was a warning. Officials told about 50,000 people in Andhra Pradesh and about 48,000 in Odisha to move to safer areas. At least 609 schools became rehabilitation centres, places where families can stay.
Sadiq, who lives in Kakinada, said the warnings helped people prepare. Many locked their homes and moved. Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu says at least seven people died.

The storm weakened by Wednesday afternoon, but it still did harm. Mr Naidu puts the early loss at Rs 4,600 crore, and says it could rise after a closer check. Around 8,000 electricity poles fell in Konaseema alone. Power was cut in nearly 400 villages.
Later, floods reached southern Odisha, where more than 100,000 people were evacuated, meaning moved away from danger.
Families who leave relief camps get 25 kilograms of rice and cash.

challenge.title: LAND ON YOUR OWN TITAN
body: Build a pretend Titan on the floor. Use cushions and books as sand dunes. One person is Dragonfly and walks slowly over the dunes with a toy. Look at the ground, pick the flattest safe spot and land the toy there. No one may tell Dragonfly where to go.

Now add a fault, which is a problem. While Dragonfly is not looking, a helper moves a cushion into the landing spot. Can Dragonfly spot the new hazard and choose another place alone? NASA's team also plans to add faults on purpose, to check that Dragonfly answers them by itself.

did_you_know.text: Swift's picture archive is open to the public. It holds more than 1.5 million ultraviolet and optical images, about 12 terabytes in all.

explainer.title: HOW A ROBOT FLIES BY ITSELF
body: Titan is far from Earth, so a pilot at home cannot steer Dragonfly in real time. The robot has to look, think and act on its own. It needs sensors that work like eyes and a sense of balance.

Dragonfly's lidar measures how high the ground is and how steep it is, and spots hazards. Two navigation cameras look at the terrain. Inertial measurement units sense how the craft moves. The computer combines these clues to choose a safe place to land. That is why engineers rehearse every sensor on the ground first.
